node.label: Daniel K Richter
node.date_label: “War and Culture: The Iroquois Experience” (1983) · The Ordeal of the Longhouse (1992) · Facing East from Indian Country (2001)
node.description: A historian of early North America who reconstructs colonial encounters from the standpoint of Native communities. In a Penn interview report he explains his decision to unsettle narratives organized around westward European settlement. His method also acknowledges the limits of reconstruction: Michael Monescalchi’s substantive reading of the Facing East prologue emphasizes contextual inference without pretending to recover another person’s vision transparently. Indigenous history here names the subject and method; it supplies no inference about the historian’s own identity.
node.representative_figures_and_works: “War and Culture: The Iroquois Experience” (1983); The Ordeal of the Longhouse (1992); Facing East from Indian Country (2001; paperback 2003).
node.scope_note: New identity matched by full name and three titles across Penn testimony and institutional CV. Own testimony and explicitly named reader support distinct methodological claims. No Indigenous identity is inferred from his subject; no namesake or P: key union. Original and paperback dates remain separate.

named_group_routes.relationship: shares attention to historical meanings while distinguishing conceptual change from situated interventions
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Comparative teaching link, not a claim that one school originated the other. Conceptual change and situated speech acts are different research problems, despite shared attention to language. Koselleck’s chapter 5 examines semantic layers and concepts/social reality, Skinner reconstructs interventions, and the French philosophe article studies social roles and pragmatic oppositions. Richter’s 1995 chapter abstracts explicitly compare these programs. This is documented comparison, not an assertion that only one program attends to context or change.

named_group_routes.relationship: Ancient unity questioned and the Chinese nation reformulated: a contested trajectory (1923–1939)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Richter describes Gu’s early challenge to a unitary ancient origin. Zheng reads the 1939 unity thesis critically; Jenco’s abstract emphasizes a politically open, plural community, while Kim’s emphasizes retreat toward homogenization. These disagreements remain explicit; no single retrospective verdict is adopted.

named_group_routes.relationship: Asks whether an alphabetical history of concepts can reconstruct the complexity of political languages and avoid projecting the historian’s categories onto earlier actors (published 1996).
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Pocock, Concepts and Discourses, pp. 47–55, especially pp. 50–55. He explicitly cannot read German and responds to Richter’s presentation of the lexicon. He welcomes a complementary conceptual history and does not dismiss Koselleck’s project or claim first-hand inspection of all its articles. The distinction is an acknowledged methodological challenge, not an assertion that Cambridge and conceptual history are mutually exclusive schools.

sources.citation: Hartmut Lehmann and Melvin Richter, eds., The Meaning of Historical Terms and Concepts: New Studies on Begriffsgeschichte (German Historical Institute, Occasional Paper 15, 1996): J. G. A. Pocock, “Concepts and Discourses,” 47–58; Reinhart Koselleck, “A Response to Comments,” 59–70.

verification.note: Official institutional full PDF. Preface pp. 5–6, Richter pp. 7–9, Pocock pp. 47–58 and Koselleck pp. 59–66 read closely; final reply pp. 67–70 consulted for concluding context. Copyright/preface date the publication to 1996; the preface dates the symposium to December 1992. Claims are dated to the published text, not assumed identical to an uncollated oral delivery. Pocock explicitly says he does not read German and responds through Richter’s presentation. His criticism of the lexicon and his particular criticism of Skinner coexist with openness to complementary methods. Koselleck argues for interdependence, not an opposition between two homogeneous schools. Other contributions and original German lexicon entries unread, except as stated. No new direct quotations.

verification.note: Read all eight pages of the available publisher introduction to Niklas Olsen, History in the Plural. Publisher listing https://v1.berghahnbooks.com/title/OlsenHistory dates hardback January 2012 and paperback February 2014. Excerpt cites a 2013 item, so exact excerpt edition is uncollated and not assumed identical to the 2012 printing. Supports attributed account of plural histories and intellectual reception. verification.note: Read title/copyright/contents, complete author preface pp. 1–5, complete chapter 5 pp. 75–92, and chapter 14 pp. 255–264, 271–275. Pages 265–270 unread; original German and cited witnesses uncollated. Supports distinctions between words/concepts, concepts/social reality and source/analytical categories, plus experience/expectation as formal categories with historically variable contents. Nietzsche quotation p. 85 and Weber typology p. 92 support particular resources, not general intellectual descent. Preface acknowledges Herder and collective lexicon work. Modernity thesis remains attributed and qualified for uneven temporalities.
